A Strategic Attitude to Architectural Design with a Culture-
Based Psychological Approach (Case Study: Public Spaces in
Kermanshah)
Parya Khandan1 · Hossein Rezaei2,3
Accepted: 6 May 2022 / Published online: 3 July 2022
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature B.V. 2022
Abstract
Recently, the quality of public spaces has become a significant issue in societies. Also,
considering the human-environment relationship, creating a high level of sense of place
through the design process can lead to efficient environments. Because each culture has a
different perception of environment, design for each environment requires understanding
the prevailing culture that can affect the components shaping the environmental affor-
dances role and the quality of place in its specific user’s mind. Therefore, this study aims
to identify the factors affecting the quality of architectural space and strengthen the sense
of place with a culture-based psychological approach. Accordingly, the main question is:
how do the physical factors affect the sense of place in public spaces under the influence
of socio-cultural currents? Thus, these factors were categorized in different perceptual-
cognitive dimensions regarding the users’ personality traits based on cultural factors. This
developmental-applied research explores prior researcher’s theories with a descriptive-
analytical method leading to an explanatory model and the resulting theory, which of
course consequently has to be validated using statistical techniques. The results show that
various cultures lead to the dominance of some personality traits, differences in mental
schemas, cognitive maps, perceptions of the environmental affordances, and consequently
different degrees of sense of place. Accordingly, considering the effect of region-specified
users’ psychological personality types on their perception of the environment’s physical
components, it is possible to design effectively, achieve the desired degrees of sense of
place, and improve the quality of life through improving the quality of space.
Keywords Physical Factors · Perceptual-Cognitive Dimensions · Cultural Currents ·
Personality Traits · Environmental Perception · Sense of Place
1 Introduction
Cities are complex systems that are constantly evolving as life changes. Meanwhile, the
importance of urban environments’ quality as the people’s main settlements is increasing

day by day. These environments are important tools for developing various indicators of
life, such as health, work, leisure, etc., and their quality should be seriously considered.
Regarding the quality of the environment, particular attention is usually paid to human life’s
material aspects, the provision and promotion of social capacities, and the development of
communities based on social behavior patterns. This has become one of the main goals of
policymakers and urban planners (Gilderbloom & Brazley, 2005). Therefore, understand-
ing the concept of environmental quality, recognizing the effective components, and trying
to achieve it in architectural spaces with respect to the changes in contemporary societies
is essential. In modern science, this concept is usually understood through mental indi-
cators resulting from citizens’ understanding and satisfaction. Among these, the meaning
is one of the main factors in measuring the environment’s quality (Kazemi & Behzadfar,
2013). Thus, considering today’s circumstances, architectural design can increase the envi-
ronment’s quality by effectively using environmental psychology knowledge. Because this
category of psychology inevitably emphasizes the need to pay equal attention to the experi-
ences, behavior, and environmental conditions of individuals (Rezaei, Keramati, Dehbashi
Sharif & Nasir Salami, 2018: a). Evidence demonstrates that there is a strong and undeni-
able relationship between individuals, their behaviors, and the architectural space around
them (Lewicka, 2011). The relationship between man and the environment is a two-way
relationship driven by perception (Nasir Salami & Sohangir, 2014). The environmental
affordances transmit information to perceive that environment, and this information is used
to perceive what the environment provides (Daneshgarmoghaddam & Eslampour, 2013). In
other words, environmental affordances are what the environment offers to its users (Gib-
son, 1977). In adaptation to human needs, a man-made environment can correspond to their
behaviors in relation to their needs. Therefore, the potential affordances of the place, fol-
lowing the mental and psychological characteristics of users, are perceived and used with
different levels (Motalebi, 2006), in a way that supports some behaviors and limits others.
Accordingly, only certain people in a given culture can understand some of the place’s
potential affordances. Other affordances may be understandable to everyone and can easily
be transformed from potential to actual. In fact, at the basic levels of environmental mean-
ings, the understanding of environmental affordances depends on man’s biological func-
tions. Also, at the level of symbolic meanings, it results from an individual’s experiences
based on socio-cultural currents and is not usually understood by all. On the other hand, the
goal of architecture and environmental design is to achieve a high level of sense of place
for users following their perception of environmental meaning and the resulting feeling
(Rezaei, 2019). This concept is an important factor in the coordination of the individuals and
their environment. Also, it leads to better utilization, user satisfaction, continued presence,
and subsequently a sense of belonging to place (Falahat, 2006). As a result, this leads to the
emergence of more effective behaviors such as creativity on the path to self-actualization
and increased quality of life (Rezaei, 2020), especially in public spaces where citizens’
social and cultural needs should be responded to (Daneshpour & Charkhchyan, 2007). Thus,
realizing the highest levels of this feeling in such spaces is essential because public spaces
are one of the most important parts shaping a city’s identity in which the greatest amount
of human interaction occurs therein (Tibbalds, 2012). These spaces are influenced by and
affect the collective life, urban culture, and people’s daily issues (Worpole, 1992). In fact,
public spaces are a reflection of cultural values and reflect the gatherings of racial groups
1 3

A Strategic Attitude to Architectural Design with a Culture-Based… 2385
and different social strata in the urban and regional areas. Thus, each society in history has
created certain social spaces to meet its cultural various needs (Hayden, 1997).
The main motivation behind this study is to improve the quality of life through improv-
ing the quality of spaces with a culture-based psychological approach. It is undeniable that
throughout history and across different cultures, attempts have always been made to shape
and respond to spaces on different scales based on cultural needs. But a significant gap is
how in today’s modern society, with vague cultural boundaries influenced by globalization
and knowledge gained in various sociological and psychological sciences, this subject can
be formulated and explained with a systemic approach. In fact, how is it possible to lead
environmental affordance in any space, especially public spaces to create a suitable environ-
ment in order to achieve a high level of sense of place for people with different personal and
socio-cultural characteristics? Also, how do the interactions, co-existence, and satisfaction
of most users of these environments improve the quality of community life? Therefore, the
main question of the present study is how socio-cultural factors affect the users’ perception
of the physical factors in public spaces, and how can this process be presented in the form
of an explanatory model? In this way, a correct understanding can be obtained of its mecha-
nism to provide paradigms in the architectural design process. Therefore, the objectives of
this study are to identify the factors affecting the architectural space quality and strengthen
the place sense with a culture-based psychological approach; to classify the physical factors
regarding the sense of place, particularly in public spaces according to perceptual-cognitive
dimensions of the human mind, and their adaptation to the basic needs of people with dif-
ferent personality traits, shaped by socio-cultural factors. In addition, this study aims to
analyze when and how individuals reach the high levels of sense of place such as place
attachment and sense of belonging in public spaces in order to improve the quality of these
places and eventually improve the quality of people’s lives.
In order to respond to the main questions, fill the gaps, achieve the main purpose, and
assess the validity of the study hypotheses, a survey was conducted on some local residents
in Kermanshah; the capital of Kermanshah province, located in the western part of Iran.
This area, which was one of the first sites of human settlements in Iran, has always been
attacked by foreigners due to its strategic location. Kermanshah is located near the border
of Iraq and was attacked 1100 times by the Iraqi government during the eight-year war
from 1980 to 1988. This war has changed the socio-cultural life of several generations of
its citizens, and its effects on people’s physics, minds, and especially personality traits are
still evident. According to some studies on the relationship between culture and personality
traits, residents in Kermanshah (known as Kurdish people) scored lower on most personal-
ity traits than other Iranian ethnic groups. Therefore, in this research, attempt has been made
to identify spatial features in the range of the people’s perception with dominant personality
traits, so that by applying them to architectural design strategies, the quality level of public
spaces and ultimately citizens’ quality of life can be increased.
2 Literature review, theoretical foundations, and framework of the
research
Many researchers have conducted research with regard to the sense of place and the main
findings should be mentioned here. Shamai (1991) in “Sense of Place: An Empirical Mea-
1 3

2386 P. Khandan, H. Rezaei
surement”, refers to the sense of place as a mixture of conscious and unconscious feelings
caused by perception. He believes that a person’s sense of place influences his attitudes and
behavior in that place. Stefanovic (1998) in “Phenomenological Encounters with Place”,
states that the sense of place is a multidimensional concept and is related to the symbolic
and emotional identification of a person towards the place. In addition, Falahat (2006) in
“The Sense of Place and Its Factors” believes that sense of place means the mental percep-
tion of people and more or less conscious feelings about the environment that puts a person
in an internal relationship with it. According to Rapoport (1990) in his book entitled “The
Meaning of the Built Environment”, in addition to the physical elements, the environment
contains messages, meanings, and codes that people understand and judge based on their
role, expectations, motivations, and other factors. As mentioned above, many researchers
have studied the field of sense of place and there is no contradiction between their views.
However, it can be said that their definitions of the subject are usually general and they have
paid less attention to details. For instance, the role of the type of space in the concept of the
sense of place has been neglected. In fact, the definition of the sense of place and its affect-
ing factors in public and private spaces may be different. According to Steele (1981), factors
that shape this feeling are divided into two categories: physical and perceptual-cognitive.
On the other hand, according to Khandan and Rezaei (2021), physical features of a place
have different perceptual-cognitive origins in users’ mind. Thus, the sense of place is real-
ized only through the perception of the environment and the judgment of what is perceived.
In this regard, Iravani & Khodapanahi (2000) in “Sensation and Perception Psychology”
consider the basis of perception as a drive for meaningfulness and believe that this factor is
influenced by values and attitudes inspired by socio-cultural conditions.
According to Smith-Walter, Jones, Shanahan & Peterson (2020), individuals view the
world through a specific filter that works to produce systematic cognitive biases. These
biases influence how people process new information. They maybe accept information that
affirms their priors (i.e. culture) or reject them. In fact, as Tam and Milfont (2020) say
in “Towards Cross-Cultural Environmental Psychology: A State-of-the-Art Review and
Recommendations”, human-environment interactions are culture-bound. Also, Reese, Oet-
tler and Katz (2019) in “Imagining the Loss of Social and Physical Place Characteristics
Reduces Place Attachment” believe that the social characteristics (like culture) of a place
seem more important than physical features in order to experience sense of place and sub-
sequently place attachment. Although, according to Khandan and Rezei (2021) the socio-
cultural characteristic and physical features of a place are not separate from each other, and
the socio-cultural characteristics of a community define how physical features should be in
order to experience a sense of place.
On the other hand, many studies have examined personality traits among different cul-
tures and countries. Lester (2000) in “National Differences in Neuroticism and Extraver-
sion” examines the personality traits among different nationalities and reports significant
differences in people’s characteristics across various ethnicities and nationalities (with
various cultures). Also, according to Shahidi, Nejati and Kamari (2015) in “The Iranian
Personality: Evidence of Cultural Differences of Personality Traits”, culture, ethnicity, and
geographical climate can affect people’s personality traits and behavior. They believe that
culture and personality are not separate issues. Also, there is a significant difference between
the various ethnic groups in all aspects of personality, which indicates the ethnic and cul-
tural effect on personality. According to recent studies, socio-cultural currents shape per-
1 3

A Strategic Attitude to Architectural Design with a Culture-Based… 2387
sonality traits and subsequently human perception. Then, what is less addressed in previous
related research is the indirect impact of socio-cultural currents on users’ perception of the
environment by intervening with the variable of personality traits that could lead to different
feelings and behaviors toward space.
With this explanation, it seems that every personality trait is stimulated and satisfied
by some external factors, and this issue should be considered in studies and in response to
human needs by the environment. Therefore, what is missing in environmental studies is
that acquisitive mental schemas that lead to perception are influenced by personality traits
and formed based on people’s culture and society. Accordingly, it can be said that the envi-
ronmental design in any geographical and temporal situation requires knowledge of the
dominant culture and personality traits of the public in the target community. Therefore, this
study aims to develop a structured and coherent framework to guide the design process in
this regard, which has not received much attention in previous research.
In the following, the theoretical foundations of the research are presented in several parts,
and then the summary and theoretical framework of the research is explained in a concep-
tual model and its resulting theory. After that, the validity of the research theory and the used
statistical methods will be discussed.
2.1 The process of perception in the human-environment relationship with an
emphasis on the concept of affordance
To transform particular objectivity into a mentality and use it as a criterion for evaluation
and behavior, individuals go through an intermediate step called “perception”, a process
of organizing and interpreting sensory data to make them meaningful (Pakzad & Bozorg,
2016). On the other hand, meaning can be understood as the sum of all mentalities created
by a stimulus for the observer, when he compares it with his experiences and goals (Rapo-
port, 1990). Various researchers have classified meaning levels. In this regard, Bourdieu
(1977) believes that each phenomenon has meanings at both primary and secondary levels.
At the primary level, the main characteristics of the phenomena are included. At the second-
ary level, their symbolic content is included. In addition, the factors affecting the forma-
tion of individuals’ different perceptions from a physical environment can be classified into
two categories, namely, individual factors and environmental factors. This research focuses
solely on studying the effect of socio-cultural factors (as an essential environmental factor)
on the perception process (given its importance).
Also, human beings have different material, psychological and spiritual motivations.
These motivations guide and organize their perception, cognition, and behavior. Human
needs, demands, and desires, as motivational factors, can be divided into functional (physi-
cal and mental) and meta-functional (spiritual). Accordingly, functional demands include
physical and psychological cases, and meta-functional desires are based on worldviews
and human belief systems (Rezaei, Keramati, Dehbashi Sharif & Nasir Salami, 2018: b).
On the other hand, according to Gibson, the affordance is what the environment provides
or makes available. In his view, affordances are not the cause of behavior but rather control
it (Gibson, 2014). Therefore, environmental affordances can provide opportunities to act
in that environment (Good, 2007). Thus, some physical environments are more capable
of providing certain behaviors (Gibson, 1977). It should be noted that not all users could
understand all the environment’s potential affordances (Motalebi, 2006). In fact, an environ-
1 3

2388 P. Khandan, H. Rezaei
ment may provide special affordances for an individual according to specific structural or
functional characteristics, while it may not do so for another (Heft, 2001). Accordingly, the
situation of individuals (in terms of their points of view such as motivations, experiences,
values or their different interpretations of environmental aesthetics) determines the extent
of their perception and use of their surroundings (Lang, 1987). Thus, contrary to Gibson’s
view that environmental affordances are fixed, pre-existing, and inexhaustible, this phenom-
enon is a joint product of a society’s physical actions and socio-cultural conditions (Good,
2007). Different users of a building at different times can request different functions based
on their wishes. Accordingly, architectural forms and spaces provide various opportunities
for human behavior so that different functional layers are proposed to the man-made space
(based on his needs) (Motalebi, 2006). Lang (1987), also, believes that in-depth percep-
tion and recognition of environmental affordances as well as human beings’ biological and
socio-cultural characteristics are important because the perception of environmental affor-
dances is a context-dependent concept and has different levels. Therefore, the expected
affordances of the design should be identified and referred to by considering the obvious
and hidden aspects of the design context, which include the characteristics of the environ-
ment (naturally, physically, socio-culturally) (Daneshgarmoghaddam & Eslampour, 2013).
2.1.1 Socio-cultural factors affecting perception in relation to different personality
traits, especially in public spaces
Individuals’ perception forms according to how meaningful a phenomenon is. This helps
the person to identify phenomena and understand their meanings. A significant part of this
meaningfulness is influenced by the values and attitudes formed under socio-cultural con-
ditions (Iravani & Khodapanahi, 2000). Socio-cultural attitudes, prejudices, thoughts and
values all determine perception. Hence, society’s socio-cultural factors and values lead to
differences in perception. This is because culture shapes people’s lives and group behavior
in the form of a dynamic process that includes social experiences, values, attitudes, norms
and shared ideas passed down from generation to generation over time (Hassim & Wagner,
2013). This concept also includes individuals’ physical, personal, and psychological char-
acteristics in each society (Zarani, Behzadpoor & Babaei, 2017). Individuals’ personality
traits evolve under the influence of various biological and environmental factors (Wechsler,
Benson, Machado, Bachert & Gums, 2018). Therefore, the prevailing culture as one of the
environmental factors has a tremendous impact on the formation and development of per-
sonality traits and psychological characteristics of individuals in society. In fact, culture is
a tool for understanding and predicting human behavior (Zarani et al., 2017). It, also, can
identify individuals prone to certain mental disorders by creating specific personality traits
(Leighton & Hughes, 2005) and lead to differences in their perceptions of the environment.
In fact, brain and body activity in response to design characteristics can occur without con-
scious perception (Bower, Tucker & Enticott, 2019). McCrae (2004), in “Big Five Personal-
ity Traits” theory, defines five personality traits for individuals based on biological reasons,
and believes that personality differences reflect their genetic differences. Thus, individuals
may follow cultural norms that are compatible with their personality. Based on this model,
individuals’ personality traits fall into one of the following categories: extraversion-intro-
version, adaptability, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness and welcoming experience.
There are other categories as well. For example, according to the model offered by Ahmadi,
1 3

A Strategic Attitude to Architectural Design with a Culture-Based… 2389
Babashahi, and Khodashenas (2011), individuals’ personality traits are classified into six
categories: extraversion-introversion, adaptability, conscientiousness, neuroticism, open-
ness and welcoming experience, and excitement-seeking. In the present study, to establish
the relationship between personality traits and their effects on understanding environmen-
tal affordances and their manifestations in architecture’s physical preferences, the “con-
scientiousness” trait was less addressed, and “excitement-seeking” and “hedonism” were
replaced.
In a brief explanation of this classification, particularly with regard to the preferences of
the physical environment, it should be noted that the introversion-extraversion character-
istic indicates the degree of individualism or sociality of individuals. Extroverts are social
and active and introverts are individualistic and balanced. Therefore, people inclined toward
extraversion in this spectrum usually prefer bright colors and crowded environments. The
adaptability attribute refers to the individual’s ability to adapt to different environmental
conditions. On the other hand, neuroticism involves a person’s emotional instability, espe-
cially in experiencing negative and unpleasant emotions. These people have less power
to control their negative emotions. In contrast, people who score low on neuroticism are
emotionally stable, calm, and self-controlled. Prominent manifestations of this trait include
anxiety, aggression, depression, feelings of inferiority, and extreme environmental vulner-
ability (Costa & McCrae, 1995). Thus, these people suffer in environments that induce feel-
ings of fear, imbalance and instability. Openness and welcoming experience indicates the
person’s interest and fascination with new phenomena and experiences. Such people are
creative, curious, and sensitive (De Bruin & Taylor, 2006). People on the other side of
the spectrum feel more comfortable under familiar circumstances. Characteristics of this
personality trait include imagination, desire for beauty, and interest in unusual actions and
experiences (McCrae & Costa, 1980). In addition, excitement-seeking relates to the expe-
rience of different emotions and includes the desire for diverse, complex, novel, unprec-
edented experiences and feelings, and passion for risk and adventure (Zuckerman, 2003).
Excitement-seeking people are more tolerant of ambiguous situations. Hedonism also indi-
cates people’s desire to enjoy more. Such people in different environments have a deeper
understanding of the environment’s positive features and better understand beauty. Thus,
they better understand the implicit meaning of the phenomena.
It is worth noting that people’s personality traits in different cultures have been studied
extensively and the influence of these traits on the prevailing cultural currents has been
confirmed. For example, the study of Shahidi et al. (2015) shows a significant difference
between all Iranian ethnic groups (with different cultures and subcultures) in terms of per-
sonality traits. The average score of the Mazani people (those who live in the north of Iran)
is higher than other ethnicities according to indices such as extraversion, hedonism, open-
ness and welcoming experience. In the case of Kurdish people (who live in the west of Iran),
it is lower than other ethnicities. In contrast, Kurdish people have the highest scores in terms
of conscientiousness and neuroticism. Accordingly, it should be noted that studying these
personality traits in accordance with the prevailing cultural currents in each region could
play an essential role in the effectiveness of assessing the users’ needs in the design process.
Specific contextual conditions, especially cultural factors, highlight individual personality
traits in people living in the area. As a result, in the face of a phenomenon, including the
architectural effect, people’s perceptions, feelings, and behaviors are likely to be directed in
a particular direction. Therefore, it can be affected in a specific way, facilitating its predic-
1 3

2390 P. Khandan, H. Rezaei
tion, thereby increasing the effectiveness of architectural strategies and actions in the design
phase. Therefore, in the design process, it is necessary to identify and determine different
perceptions based on culture and consequently different personality traits of people in the
target community, and thus act according to them to promote a sense of place.
Also, it should be noted that according to previous research, some socio-cultural differ-
ences affect the access to and perception of public spaces, and that different socio-cultural
groups have different perceptions of the city (Arefi & Meyers, 2003). This issue is even
more critical in relation to Iran’s current situation, where most public spaces lack functional-
ity. In fact, the quality of social life is determined in these spaces and they reflect citizens’
value for their society (Calthorpe, 1993). Obviously, judgments about the quality of pub-
lic spaces go back to individuals’ perception. They, influenced by their environmental and
cultural aspects, evaluate environmental factors differently from each other. According to
Gibson (1977), an environment proposes something (the environments affordance) (Lang,
1987), and the understanding of its affordance is based on the user’s characteristics, experi-
ences, competencies, and needs (Rezaei, Keramati & Dehbashi Sharif, 2018). Therefore, the
local user’s judgment from a public space is more important than the judgments of people
who do not use that place continuously.
2.1.2 Sense of place formation and its shaping factors
From a physical perspective, each place is a part of space that is perceived and expressed
by different senses. Therefore, it expresses certain values and meaning that is created by the
interaction of people and the environment (Falahat, 2006). In other words, every meaningful
physical position is called a place (Lewicka, 2011). Place refers to any space that becomes
meaningful in an individual or group cultural process (Low & Altman, 1992). Also, authors
in many fields have explicitly distinguished “place” from “location”, with “location” invok-
ing the objective aspect, and “place” adding a connotation of subjectivity and feeling (Zia,
Norton, Metcalf, Hirsch & Hannon, 2014). In the process of perceiving the environment,
human beings evaluate the information obtained from different senses through their central
processing system. After judging it, they develop specific feelings toward the physical envi-
ronment (which can be positive or negative) called the sense of place which can shape their
behavior. In fact, their personal behavior is expressed as a response and reaction to the envi-
ronment. Therefore, it can be acknowledged that the sense of place is an essential factor in
realizing socio-cultural relations in a particular place, recalling experiences and memories,
and finding identity. As a result, it transforms a space into a place with unique sensory and
behavioral characteristics.
According to Steele (1981), the most important physical factors that create a sense of
place are size, enclosure degree, contrast, scale, distance, texture, color, and visual diversity.
Also, natural elements (Salvesen, 2002) and how a place relates to environment (Bonaiuto,
Fornara & Bonnes, 2003; Lansing, Marans & Zehner, 1970) are effective in creating a sense
of place. In explaining this feeling, Shamai (1991) considers seven levels, including indif-
ference to the place, awareness of it, belonging, attachment, unification with its goals, com-
mitment, and sacrifice for the place, with most emphasis on the three positive features of
belonging, attachment, and commitment. When these three are dominant, the mentioned
physical factors mainly manifest in the form of spatial features and environmental affor-
dances that can be studied in different perceptual-cognitive dimensions. These dimensions
1 3

A Strategic Attitude to Architectural Design with a Culture-Based… 2391
are related to individuals’ mental processes formed in biological, psychological, and envi-
ronmental contexts, influenced by socio-cultural currents (Falahat, 2006). The source for
human perception of the environment can often be studied from three dimensions: opera-
tional, reactive-emotional, and inferential. In addition, each of them is a specific aspect of
the physical environment corresponding to different human needs (Golkar, 2001). There-
fore, the physical factors of place are perceived with one perceptual-cognitive origin or a
combination of them. Thus, a spatial feature, depending on the situation, may have several
perceptual-cognitive origins. In this study, each spatial feature is placed in one perceptual-
cognitive category that is perceived more by that origin. A person’s feelings toward a place
not only express his emotions, understanding, and beliefs about the physical features but
also represent his perception and the way he acts and behaves in that place. Also, behavioral
tendencies in the place represent the behavioral aspect of that place in response to cognition
(Jorgensen & Stedman, 2001). Therefore, cultural currents in guiding and cultivating mental
schemas, as well as the different influences of perceptual origins from external factors and
stimuli, are influential factors in realizing the sense of place for users.
2.2 Conceptual model
As mentioned earlier, by being in a place, a user establishes a conscious or unconscious
connection with it. The information he receives from the environment and the process of its
perception is influenced by their needs, demands, desires, mental schemas, and personality
traits, all of which should be related to the socio-cultural factors of the environment. First,
the user tries to understand the physical factors of the environment (spatial features) by
operational, reactive-emotional, or inferential perceptual mechanisms. Then, the affordances
of the environment are evaluated and exploited based on personality traits, based on which
meaning of the environment is realized. The resulting meaning can be placed in one of two
levels of explicit or implicit meaning, the continuation and reinforcement of which leads to
the formation of environmental attributes in the user’s mind. Perception of physical mean-
ings (explicit meaning), particularly abstract meanings (implicit and symbolic meaning),
mainly related to personal and socio-cultural mentalities, can lead to a semantic presence in
place and a strong connection between a person and the environment. It ultimately creates a
sense of place and possibly the realization of high levels such as attachment, commitment,
and sacrifice. Early levels, which are perceived consciously or unconsciously, indicate a
person’s superficial and normal familiarity with the place and create a positive or negative
feeling toward the place. In contrast, secondary levels are more collective and cultural.
Understanding the symbols of the place is mainly done subconsciously, which indicates
a deep familiarity with the place and leads to a positive feeling toward it. On the second
level, the influence of the cultural factor may be observed. Therefore, in addition to paying
attention to the physical factors that lead to the perception of basic and apparent meanings,
physical factors based on socio-cultural influences must be addressed. A high level of sense
of place must then be realized by guiding and purposefully adjusting the design process in
spaces by recognizing the processes of cognition based on personality traits influenced by
culture and, consequently, how mental schemas and cognitive maps of different people are
affected. In light of this argument, we can describe the variables studied in this research as
follows (variables that depend on effectiveness of knowledge and profession of architecture
or any environmental design). The independent variable includes the physical features of
1 3

the environment and architectural measures to create and purposefully adjust the mentioned
factors in accordance with the perceptual-cognitive dimensions of place perception. Users’
environmental perception is considered as an intervening variable. Besides, users’ personal-
ity traits, and socio-cultural indicators of society (with mutual communication and strong
correlation) are considered moderating variables (another group of independent variables
with a mechanism of intensifying or weakening the relationships). Finally, the possible lev-
els of realization of the sense of place are introduced as a dependent variable. Accordingly,
as mentioned earlier, adapting the physical factors of any place to the perceptual-cognitive
dimensions and examining the role of personality traits, helps to understand the user’s needs
and their environmental preferences by focusing on the influence of cultural currents in
each region. It also refers to the fact that the mainstream culture affects the formation of
personality traits or establishing the dominant personality types of the majority of people

Rezaei et al., 2020). According to another article by Rezaei et al. (2018: b), spatial features
were classified into two categories in terms of type: functional (mainly physical) and meta-
functional (spiritual), both with important psychological effects, to allow the most accurate
recognition of the perceptual-cognitive dimensions of them. Therefore, in Fig. 1, how a
place’s physical factors adapt to its perceptual-cognitive dimensions based on individuals’

how the problem variables are related in the form of a conceptual model. With this expla-

consequently, the desired environmental attributes of each one, based on the aggregation

personality traits feel more needed than some spatial features. Therefore, they demand dif-
ferent environmental affordances that can be achieved by combining these features regard-
ing their desired environmental attributes. Due to the overlap of many spatial features in
shaping different environmental affordances, only ones with higher priority and stronger
impact on each personality trait were addressed here. The corresponding environmental
affordances were also proposed so that they have the most relationship with the mentioned
spatial features. The mind’s perceptual-cognitive origins and the influence of a particular
personality type (a particular combination of the intensity and weakness of personality traits
influenced by environmental conditions, especially prevailing socio-cultural currents) on
mental schemas can be examined from a specific use in a specific geographical area for the
general users. Accordingly, it is possible to present architectural design goals and strategies
to combine spatial features and create specific environmental affordances. Consequently,
this has an impact on their synergy to establish the desired environmental attributes in any
place, including public spaces. In addition, the personality traits discussed in this article are
unique to all individuals with different values. Their outcome leads to the formation of a
dominant personality type, which usually according to the dominant culture and the specific
type of users, could be predicted. Also, special users of any particular building can be sur-
veyed in the design phase.
3 Methodology
The present research is a developmental-applied one in terms of its purpose and it has been
carried out to classify and adapt spatial features to the perceptual-cognitive dimensions of
forming the sense of place in the user’s mind. This is particularly the case in terms of the
impact of socio-cultural currents on the creation and stabilization of personality traits. In
the following, the method and process of conducting the research are described in four sec-
tions: Measures, Sample, Questionnaire, and Techniques. In the first section of this part the
variables have been discussed. In the next section, the method of sampling, the process of
randomization, the response rate, and the number of surveys carried out will be discussed.
In the following, the questionnaire will be analyzed in detail, and in the last section, the
techniques used and why they are used will be explained.

3.1 Measures
As a theoretical framework, a descriptive-analytical method and logical reasoning were
used to examine and explain the relationships between the variables and finally to refine the
hypothesis and theories. This study focused more on practical features that have the poten-
tial to be implemented in architectural design. In the next step, to test the hypothesis and
confirm the output of the previous step, quantitative surveys were carried out. In this step,
to collect the analyzable data, a researcher-made questionnaire was prepared based on the
theoretical framework and the conceptual model. The results were intended to answer the
basic research question on how to study and judge the spatial features of the environment in
the perceptual-cognitive process of public space in users’ minds according to their personal-
ity traits influenced by the region’s culture. The research was carried out using case studies
strategy and measuring people’s opinions about the studied samples.
In the process of adapting physical features of the environment with their perceptual-
cognitive origins in user’s mind and eventually the realization of sense of place in public
spaces, many variables were considered. The physical features of the environment and their
adaptability to the perceptual-cognitive aspects were considered as an independent vari-
able. Users’ environmental perception as an intervening variable, socio-cultural indicators
of each region as a modifier, and the sense of place as a dependent variable, were consid-
ered in the process. As will be described in detail in the questionnaire section, each of the
independent variables is presented in the form of a question in the questionnaire to measure
its importance in users’ minds. Also, the representation of each variable in the case studies
is presented in the form of a photo or diagram in each question so that the users can easily
select the best representation of that variable from the case studies and rate it.
3.2 Sample
The case study of the research focuses on the architecture of public spaces in Kermanshah
(researchers’ residence). It focuses on six landmarks of this city that have a large number
of users which makes for a reliable sample for research. The statistical population was the
people of Kermanshah as users of this building. Using Cochran’s formula and a significance
level of 90%, the sample size was 96, which can be justified given the research’s time con-
straints. 110 questionnaires were distributed; there were a few unacceptable and 96 of them
were acceptable, so the response rate was 0.87. Sampling was also conducted randomly,
and the samples had the same probability of being selected. Cases were selected from indi-
viduals over 18 years of age, including equal number of men and women. In fact, on two
consecutive days (both on weekend and a weekday), questionnaires were distributed simul-
taneously in all the buildings under review. The questionnaire was given to the first user, and
the distribution was randomized in terms of coefficient 5. In other words, the first, fifth, etc.
of the visitors who came into the buildings were surveyed. Therefore, 110 questionnaires
(96 of them were acceptable), each with two parts, were provided to individuals.
3.3 Questionnaire
The first part of the questionnaire included questions about how the physical factors of
research in public spaces, in general, were imagined. Respondents were asked to rate each

3.4 Techniques
It should be noted that classifying the spatial features in the form of functional and meta-
functional types with different perceptual origins, as well as determining the features affect-
ing the formation of environmental affordances and attributes have been concluded using
another survey, in which the authors employed Correlation and Regression techniques in
its process of analysis. The obtained data from the questionnaire were analyzed and the
research hypothesis was validated. The obtained data were entered into SPSS software ver-
sion 23, and after ensuring that the data were normal, a one-sample T-test was used to
analyze the significance of the obtained results. In justifying the use of the T-test, it can be
said that in addition to the nature and type of questions, one of the most important aspects
of the research is the Post-Occupancy Evaluation (POE) of buildings from the perspective
of citizens. About POE, it is necessary to determine the significance of people’s tendencies
in various items by comparing the average scores against the predetermined specific levels
of very low, low, medium, high, and very high (Zohreh & Rezaei, 2020). In the process
of designing buildings, especially public buildings, the region-based dominant personality
traits of users are usually not considered. Thus, by employing the concept of POE, feedback
on the performance of public buildings in use can be obtained from the perspective of users
and understand the dominant personality traits of the target community. In this process, the
T-test could be more effective to interpret the meaningfulness of results and considering the
bias errors in research analysis. Regarding this, any immediate problems are highlighted and
can be addressed, many lessons are provided that can be used to improve the design process
and procurement on future projects, which can act as benchmarking aid to compare across
projects and also over time. All of these improve user satisfaction and place productivity.
So, as mentioned, the T-test was applied to compare the average sample scores with the
hypothetical average desired for the community. The aim was to test the hypothesis in terms
of the importance of the resulting physical factors and to rank the success of each of the
studied spaces in meeting the psychological needs of the dominant personality type of city
residents. Based on this, several suggestions can be presented regarding the architectural
design process of public spaces in Kermanshah in the future. In other words, the first part
included an initial assessment of the degree of the psychological importance of the variables
for the respondents in the specific cultural context of the region. Therefore, an importance
ratio was assigned to each of them, indicating the degree of preference of each under the

4 Case study (six prominent public spaces in Kermanshah city)
Kermanshah located in the west of Iran with Kermanshah as the capital city is a vast plain
among the rugged foothills, which has provided a suitable bed for crossing regional high-
ways. Range and arable lands, suitable climate, and sufficient rainfall have been important
factors in its formation. Archaeological evidence shows that this area is one of the first
human habitats and one of the habitats in the Middle Zagros Mountains. The citizens are
mainly of Aryan Kurdish descent (ancient Iranian plateau inhabitants) and the majority are
Muslim. Since its formation, this region has always been exposed to foreign invasions due

6 Discussion
Following the emergence of environmental psychology, especially in recent years, much
research has been done regarding the sense of place by international researchers such as
Rapoport, Relph, Steele, Shamai, Stefanovic, and Iranian scholars such as Einifar, Motal-
lebi, and Falahat. They believe that a sense of place arises from the perception of physical
factors, meanings, and messages of an environment. This feeling puts them in an internal
connection with the place and influences their spatial behaviors. They have attempted to
identify and classify the levels of sense of place and its shaping factors. As the result, it
is acknowledged that the physical factors of a place such as size, scale, texture, and color
are factors that their combination in a synergic whole shape the sense of place in people’s
minds. They also define different levels of a sense of place, from disgust with a place to
sacrifice for it. There is also an emphasis on assessing user’s needs in an environment in
the design phase and meeting their needs. On the other hand, Rapoport (1990) has consid-
ered “culture” an effective component in the process of realizing the sense of place, so it
is necessary to pay attention to it in the design process. However, no systematic research
has sought to explain the relationship between cultural, and psychological variables as well
as personality characteristics of individuals regarding their needs and preferences for the
physical environment, and then provide the spatial features that provide it. Therefore, there
is a significant difference between this research and other studies. This study has a practical
approach to the subject, also a systematic and hierarchical scrutiny of spatial features, envi-
ronmental affordances, and attributes affecting the sense of place, especially in important
public spaces. That is, in addition to providing a complete explanation of the concept of the
sense of place and how it is formed, this research suggests related spatial features and their
combination to aimfully form the environmental affordances and attributes that lead to a
high level of sense of place in users’ minds in confronting any architectural work, particu-
larly public spaces. It should be noted that these suggestions are absolutely practical and

accurately express the nature of particular spatial features and how they participate to create
environmental affordances and establish environmental attributes. Also, it classifies spatial
features based on different types and perception-cognitive origins to meet users’ psychologi-
cal needs and preferences, which is possible by knowing users’ dominant personality traits
in the specified cultural context. In fact, attempts have been made to consider “culture” as
a key component in the process of perceiving and recognizing the physical environment.
Therefore, we investigated its direct effect on the personality traits of individuals in soci-
ety and its indirect effect on judgment and interpretation of spatial features, environmental
affordances, and subsequent attributes in a particular place. Regarding the results, the initial
hypothesis of the research was confirmed. Accordingly, the cultural currents of a society
lead to the formation of dominant personality traits in people. These personality traits play
a decisive role in the formation of individuals’ perceptual-cognitive systems, mental sche-
mas, and cognitive maps, and eventually provide them with a different understanding of the
environment. This makes people in each area have a different perception of the surroundings
and therefore prefer different spatial features. This research proved that by identifying the
dominant personality traits in the people of each region, it is possible to identify appropriate
spatial features, environmental affordances, and attributes that by considering them in the
design process of public spaces, a high level of sense of place can be achieved so that the
qualitative level of spaces and citizens’ life quality can be improved.
7 Conclusions
According to previous research on environmental psychology, the present study developed
a useful guideline to increase the architectural quality, especially of public spaces. Also, to
achieve high degrees of sense of place in accordance with the prevailing cultural context and
psychological needs of the target population by setting and refining goals and strategies in
the architectural design process. Therefore, the main purpose of this study was to adapt and
categorize the spatial features according to the type and perceptual-cognitive dimensions
of the user’s mind. In addition, this research attempted to explain that the appropriateness
of environmental affordances and attributes in meeting the psychological needs of differ-
ent personality traits were greatly influenced by culture. Therefore, the present research is
a developmental-applied type in terms of purpose. The first step leads to a comprehensive
explanatory model by exploring the theories of previous researchers and a codified descrip-
tive-analytical method. In the next step, people were surveyed about some of the studied
buildings using the case study strategy. Finally, quantitative analysis of the obtained data
has been done to validate the model and research hypothesis. Also, to obtain exploratory
results based on the buildings’ architectural effectiveness that determines the necessities of
the architectural design strategy making for future. Therefore, answering the research ques-
tion, how to realize the sense of place regarding the impact of socio-cultural currents of con-
text on establishing the dominant personality traits in citizens, is explained by an emphasis
on the relative perception of place by different people. Accordingly, physical factors have
been classified according to their type and perceptual-cognitive dimensions and their aggre-
gation in the form of environmental affordances and subsequent formation of environmental
attributes to meet the user’s specific needs. Based on this mechanism, socio-cultural factors
have significant direct and indirect effects on the development and spectrum of personality

In the survey part of the research, six landmarks of public spaces in Kermanshah were
studied. A researcher-made composite questionnaire (including expressive and visual ques-
tions) was prepared based on the theoretical framework and system of research variables
and was given to 110 users (96 of them were acceptable) of the aforementioned buildings.
The questions were to assess the degree of physical factors in the selected samples and
the level of users’ satisfaction with the buildings’ overall architecture, especially from a
psychological perspective. The collected data from the questionnaires were processed by
SPSS software. After ensuring their normal distribution, a one-sample T-test was used. The
obtained information was analyzed, and the results were presented in the form of tables and
graphs. The main hypothesis of the research was confirmed and based on this, it can be said
that various physical factors in the public spaces of Kermanshah have different degrees of
importance for the region’s residents. Influenced by their particular culture and dominant
personality traits, they demand different physical components in their city buildings. This
case study showed that most Kermanshah residents are affected by their ethnic and tribal
culture as well as the profound and lasting effects of Iran-Iraq war. They rank low in terms
of extroversion, hedonism, openness, and excitement-seeking, moderate in terms of adapt-
ability, and high in terms of conscientiousness and neuroticism. Therefore, satisfying psy-
chological needs based on their culture required the provision of spatial features to establish
the environmental attributes of formal and functional balance, durability and consistency,
individualism, and justifiability. This was made possible by developing affordances such
as presence-ability, security, changeability and adaptability, activity-ability, possibility of
rest and relaxation, possibility of personalization and being dominated, being sanctimo-
nious, memorability and memory-making. In general, some of them may not be a priority
for designers by default. Therefore, physical factors with the perceptual origin and type of
“operational” and “functional”, “operational” and “meta-functional”, “reactive-emotional”
and “functional”, “reactive-emotional” and “meta-functional”, “inferential” and “meta-
functional”, and finally, “inferential” and “functional”, respectively, should be considered
to provide the mentioned affordances in the design process of future projects in this area.
It is necessary to say that the results of this research can be used in two sections related to
buildings in the operation phase and buildings that are in the initial design stage. Problems
and weaknesses of buildings in the operation phase can be identified using the concept of
POE and the results of this study to improve their current condition. Solutions can also be
found to avoid such problems in the construction of future buildings. As a result of applying
these items in buildings in the operation phase, users’ and staff satisfaction and their sense
of place attachment can increase, buildings’ performance and workplace productivity can
improve, and it could be a cost-effective solution to improve the quality of the place. The
results of this research can also be used for evidence-based designs. In other words, by rec-
ognizing the socio-cultural currents of the target community and examining the personality
and psychological characteristics of the citizens, a suitable practical model can be proposed
for use in the design strategies of a building with a specific use. Applying the results of this
research to evidence-based designs can increase the sense of place and belonging in build-
ings, improve the performance of spaces, and increase the quality of spaces. Also, using
